title: Error Mitigation From a Single Unmodified Error-Corrected Circuit
authors: Maor Shutman, Dorit Aharonov, Itai Arad, Yosi Atia, Eyal Bairey, Zvika Brakerski, Barak A. Katzir, Netanel H. Lindner, Omri Golan, Ilya Gurwich
abstract: Recent work has shown that syndrome information obtained during error-corrected quantum computation can be utilized for logical error mitigation (LEM), yielding exponential reductions in runtime overhead compared to external'' LEM methods, which do not make use of syndrome data. However, these syndrome-aware LEM methods (SALEM) generally require adaptive circuit operations based on real-time processing of syndromes. Here, we introduce syndrome-based offline logical error mitigation (SOLEM), a framework that utilizes syndrome data entirely in post-processing, without any modification to the given error-corrected circuit. In this sense, SOLEM is built into'' error-corrected circuits, and is in fact simpler to implement than external LEM protocols. The basic idea of SOLEM is to use naturally occurring syndrome-conditioned logical error channels in place of deliberate circuit modifications. We develop unbiased and heuristic estimators within this framework, including offline logical versions of probabilistic error cancellation (PEC) and zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE), as well as a global-regression estimator. SOLEM's fully offline nature leads to three significant advantages. First, SOLEM can post-process syndromes with a more powerful decoder than the one used in real time. Second, multiple estimators can be constructed from the same measured data and optimized using empirical statistical errors and related performance metrics. Third, logical error characterization is needed only in post-processing, allowing characterization data to be collected during circuit execution and reducing sensitivity to hardware drift. Remarkably, SOLEM estimators can achieve these advantages while attaining a runtime overhead which is exponentially lower than that of external LEM and is comparable to that of corresponding SALEM estimators.
summary: This paper introduces Syndrome-Based Offline Logical Error Mitigation (SOLEM), a novel framework for improving quantum computation fidelity. SOLEM processes syndrome data entirely in post-processing, avoiding the need to modify the error-corrected circuit itself. This approach offers significant advantages in implementation simplicity and performance, achieving state-of-the-art error mitigation overheads.
main_problem: Developing efficient methods for Logical Error Mitigation (LEM) in error-corrected quantum computation that do not require modifying the underlying error-corrected circuit.
main_result: The proposed Syndrome-Based Offline LEM (SOLEM) framework achieves error mitigation with an overhead exponentially lower than external methods and comparable to adaptive methods.
method: SOLEM utilizes syndrome data entirely in post-processing to construct estimators (like SOLEM-PEC, SOLEM-ZNE, SOLEM-GR) that estimate ideal logical expectation values from measured syndrome records.
model_or_system: The work is situated in the context of error-corrected quantum computation, specifically using circuits based on the Steane code, [[7, 1, 3]].
key_observables: Ideal logical expectation values ($\langle O angle$), syndrome records ($s$), and final measurement outcomes ($o$).
important_parameters: Physical error rate ($\epsilon$), syndrome-averaged logical error rate ($\epsilon_L$), and the sampling overhead ($\lambda$).
main_assumptions: SOLEM assumes that syndrome-conditioned expectation values can estimate ideal logical expectation values, and the estimators are shown to be unbiased in certain solvable models.
figures_summary: Figure 1 conceptually compares ExtLEM, SALEM, and SOLEM protocols. Figure 2 shows circuit-level simulations comparing SOLEM estimators against ideal values using Physical-to-Logical Characterization. Figure 3 compares the workflow of SOLEM against ExtLEM and SALEM.
paper_structure: The paper introduces SOLEM as a post-processing framework, develops specific estimators (PEC, ZNE, GR), and validates them through circuit-level simulations and analytical modeling of error channels.
why_interesting: It provides a practical, implementable, and theoretically robust method for improving quantum computation fidelity by leveraging syndrome data without incurring the overhead or complexity of real-time adaptive circuits.
